title: 16 — Statistics for Data Quality and Drift
html:
16 — Statistics for Data Quality and Drift

The one idea: most quality checks are fixed rules ("NAV must be positive"). Drift checks ask a different question: does today's data look like normal data? Answering it takes a few simple statistics, chosen so that one bad value can't hide itself by distorting the measure.

1. What it is

Measure Compares Output Typical use
Population stability index (PSI) Shares of values per bin, baseline vs current One number. Rule of thumb: below 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, above 0.25 significant Whole-column distribution drift, for example monthly returns or rating mix
Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistic Largest gap between two cumulative distributions 0 to 1, compared with a critical value or a p-value Has the shape changed, not just the average?
z-score Distance from the mean, in standard deviations Unbounded Quick outlier flag, when the data has no outliers yet
Robust z-score (median and MAD) Distance from the median, in units of median absolute deviation Unbounded. Above about 3.5 is a common cut-off Outliers when outliers may already be present
Seasonal baseline Same weekday, month-end, or day of the reporting cycle Expected range Volumes and arrivals that follow a calendar

The PSI bands are conventions, not standards. Sources present them as rules of thumb, and the right threshold depends on your data and on how costly a false alarm is compared with a miss.

2. Why it matters

  • Drift is one of the five quality checks in a quality gate (schema, range, consistency, drift, cross-source).
  • A plain mean and standard deviation are pulled towards the very outlier you are hunting. A misplaced decimal point can hide itself.
  • Fixed thresholds break on seasonal data: month-end volumes are not anomalies.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Pick the baseline carefully

  • A clean, approved period, not "the last 30 days", which may already include the problem.
  • The same calendar context: compare month-ends with month-ends, and Mondays with Mondays.
  • Versioned: store the baseline's period and its statistics with the rule, so a past alert can be explained.

3.2 Choose the measure by the question

---
title: Which drift measure for which question
---
flowchart TD
    Q["What changed?"] --> ONE{"One value looks wrong?"}
    ONE -- "yes" --> RZ["Robust z-score<br/>(median and MAD)"]
    ONE -- "no" --> DIST{"Whole distribution?"}
    DIST -- "share per bucket matters<br/>(e.g. rating mix)" --> PSI["PSI with fixed bins"]
    DIST -- "any change of shape" --> KS["KS statistic"]
    DIST -- "volume or arrival" --> SEAS["Seasonal baseline<br/>(same weekday or cycle day)"]

3.3 Large samples make everything significant

With hundreds of thousands of rows, KS p-values flag tiny, harmless differences. Judge the size of the change (the KS statistic itself, or PSI) against a business tolerance, not only the p-value.

3.4 From statistic to action

A drift breach in a quality gate should usually hold the rows back for review, not block the batch. Drift means "unusual", not "wrong". Attach the statistic, the baseline period and a sample of the outlying values to the exception, so the reviewer can decide quickly.

4. Working code

The script compares a baseline month of made-up daily returns with a month from the same process and with a month where volatility doubled, using PSI and KS. It then shows how a misplaced decimal point hides from a plain z-score but not from a robust one. Standard library only.

import math, random, statistics

random.seed(7)
# Made-up daily NAV returns (%) for a fund category: a calm baseline month, then two candidate months.
baseline = [random.gauss(0.05, 0.6) for _ in range(500)]
same     = [random.gauss(0.05, 0.6) for _ in range(500)]
shifted  = [random.gauss(0.05, 1.4) for _ in range(500)]     # volatility more than doubled

# 1. Population stability index (PSI): compare the share of values per bin, baseline vs current.
def psi(expected, actual, bins=10):
    qs = sorted(expected)
    edges = [qs[int(len(qs) * i / bins)] for i in range(1, bins)]          # decile edges from the baseline
    def shares(xs):
        counts = [0] * bins
        for x in xs:
            counts[sum(x > e for e in edges)] += 1
        return [max(c / len(xs), 1e-4) for c in counts]                      # floor avoids log(0)
    e, a = shares(expected), shares(actual)
    return sum((ai - ei) * math.log(ai / ei) for ei, ai in zip(e, a))

# 2. Two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic: the largest gap between the two cumulative distributions.
def ks(x, y):
    x, y = sorted(x), sorted(y)
    i = j = 0
    d = 0.0
    while i < len(x) and j < len(y):
        if x[i] <= y[j]: i += 1
        else: j += 1
        d = max(d, abs(i / len(x) - j / len(y)))
    return d
ks_critical = 1.36 * math.sqrt((500 + 500) / (500 * 500))                   # about 5% significance, large samples

def band(v):
    return "no drift" if v < 0.1 else "moderate" if v < 0.25 else "SIGNIFICANT"
for name, cur in (("same process", same), ("volatility shift", shifted)):
    p, d = psi(baseline, cur), ks(baseline, cur)
    print(f"{name:17s} PSI={p:.3f} ({band(p)})  KS={d:.4f} ({'differs' if d > ks_critical else 'same'}, critical {ks_critical:.4f})")

# 3. One bad value: a robust z-score (median and MAD) is not dragged by the outlier it is looking for.
navs = [142.10, 142.35, 142.20, 142.85, 142.60, 142.95, 1428.50, 143.10]    # a misplaced decimal point
med = statistics.median(navs)
mad = statistics.median(abs(v - med) for v in navs)
mean, sd = statistics.mean(navs), statistics.pstdev(navs)
for v in (1428.50, 143.10):
    robust = 0.6745 * (v - med) / mad
    plain = (v - mean) / sd
    print(f"value {v:8.2f}: plain z={plain:5.2f}  robust z={robust:8.2f}")

Output:

same process      PSI=0.045 (no drift)  KS=0.0560 (same, critical 0.0860)
volatility shift  PSI=0.744 (SIGNIFICANT)  KS=0.2320 (differs, critical 0.0860)
value  1428.50: plain z= 2.65  robust z= 2312.68
value   143.10: plain z=-0.38  robust z=    0.67

What to notice:

  • The same process scores PSI 0.045 and KS 0.0560, both under their thresholds. The volatility shift scores PSI 0.744 and KS 0.2320, far over. The mean didn't change, so a check on the average alone would have missed it.
  • The 1428.50 NAV (a decimal slip from 142.85) gets a plain z of only 2.65, under the usual 3, because it inflated the standard deviation itself. The robust z-score is over 2,000.
  • 1.36 × sqrt((n + m) / (n × m)) is the standard large-sample approximation of the KS critical value at about 5% significance.

5. Common mistakes

  1. A baseline that contains the problem. Use an approved, clean period.
  2. Mean and standard deviation on dirty data. Use median and MAD.
  3. Re-binning every run. PSI needs bins fixed from the baseline, or the numbers can't be compared.
  4. Trusting p-values on huge samples. Judge the size of the change.
  5. Blocking a batch on drift alone. Hold the rows back and send them for review. Drift is not proof of error.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

  1. Add a fourth month where the mean shifts by 0.3 but volatility stays the same, and see which measure reacts more.
  2. Compute PSI on a made-up rating mix (AAA, AA, A, BBB, below) for two quarters, using the categories as bins.
  3. Add a seasonal baseline: compare each weekday's row count only with the same weekday in the previous eight weeks.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why does a plain z-score miss the 1428.50 value?
  2. What do the PSI bands 0.1 and 0.25 mean, and are they a standard?
  3. When is KS more useful than PSI?
  4. Why should bins be fixed from the baseline?
  5. What should a drift breach do in a quality gate?

Answers

  1. The outlier inflates the mean and standard deviation it is measured against, so it looks less extreme.
  2. Rules of thumb: under 0.1 stable, 0.1 to 0.25 moderate, over 0.25 significant. They are conventions, not a standard.
  3. When any change of shape matters, not just shifts between predefined buckets.
  4. So that the current period is measured on the same scale as the baseline.
  5. Usually hold the affected rows back for review, with the statistic and baseline attached, rather than block the batch.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26 through web search. The PSI bands are commonly cited conventions, not a formal standard.

  • PSI bands (Alibaba Cloud PAI documentation): https://help.aliyun.com/en/pai/population-stability-index
  • Data drift measures (MetricGate docs): https://metricgate.com/docs/de/data-drift/
  • Two-sample KS test (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook): https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35g.htm
